clinicalPearls: The most common and most serious life-threatening complication of Hirschsprung disease, occurring both before and after definitive pull-through surgery.
Presents with abdominal distension, explosive foul-smelling and often bloody diarrhoea, fever, vomiting and lethargy, and can progress rapidly to sepsis, toxic megacolon and perforation.
It may be the presenting feature of previously undiagnosed Hirschsprung disease in a neonate.
Risk factors include long-segment or total colonic aganglionosis, trisomy 21, a prior HAEC episode and delayed diagnosis.
Explosive release of gas and stool on digital rectal examination is a classic sign.
The cornerstones of management are prompt fluid resuscitation, colonic decompression by rectal irrigation and washouts, bowel rest, and broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic cover.
Recurrent HAEC prompts evaluation for mechanical obstruction, residual or transition-zone aganglionosis and internal anal sphincter achalasia.
Refractory disease may require intrasphincteric botulinum toxin, anal myectomy or redo pull-through, and a diverting stoma in severe cases.
reference.pathophysiology: HAEC is a multifactorial inflammatory disorder superimposed on the functional obstruction of aganglionic bowel. Absence of ganglion cells produces tonic contraction and failure of relaxation of the affected segment, causing proximal faecal stasis and distension. Stasis, together with an abnormal intestinal mucin layer, impaired mucosal barrier function, defective innate mucosal immunity including altered secretory IgA and defensins, and intestinal dysbiosis, permits bacterial overgrowth, adherence and translocation across a compromised epithelium. The resulting mucosal invasion and inflammatory cascade drive crypt inflammation and ulceration and, in severe cases, transmural inflammation with the risk of toxic dilatation, perforation and systemic sepsis.
additionalDifferentials: Infective gastroenteritis or Clostridioides difficile colitis
Anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal abscess after pull-through
Cow's milk protein enterocolitis or food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiograph for bowel dilatation, air-fluid levels, a rectosigmoid cut-off, pneumatosis or free air
Full blood count, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, blood gas and lactate to assess sepsis and dehydration
Blood cultures and stool studies including Clostridioides difficile testing
Contrast enema to define the transition zone, avoided during acute severe colitis because of perforation risk
Rectal suction biopsy for ganglion cells where Hirschsprung disease is not yet confirmed
Examination under anaesthesia and anorectal manometry for obstructive causes in recurrent disease
Water-soluble contrast study to assess the anastomosis and exclude stricture or leak after surgery
redFlags: Fever, lethargy, tachycardia and other signs of sepsis or shock
Marked abdominal distension with tenderness, guarding or peritonism
Bloody, explosive diarrhoea with rapid clinical deterioration
Bilious vomiting with features of toxic megacolon
Pneumatosis intestinalis or free intraperitoneal air on imaging indicating perforation
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition and treatment most episodes resolve, but HAEC remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in Hirschsprung disease; episodes may recur, and severe or delayed-treated disease carries a risk of toxic megacolon, perforation and death.
pitfalls: Attributing distension and diarrhoea to simple gastroenteritis and missing HAEC in a child with, or at risk of, Hirschsprung disease.
Delaying rectal decompression and irrigation while awaiting investigations.
Performing a contrast enema during acute severe colitis and precipitating perforation.
Assuming that a successful pull-through excludes HAEC, as it can occur postoperatively and sometimes years later.
Failing to investigate an anatomical or obstructive cause after recurrent episodes.
references: American Pediatric Surgical Association guidance on the management of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis
management: Prompt intravenous fluid resuscitation with correction of electrolyte disturbance
Colonic decompression by rectal irrigation and saline washouts
Bowel rest with nasogastric decompression for distension and vomiting
Broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic cover such as metronidazole
Close monitoring for toxic megacolon, perforation and sepsis, escalating to emergency laparotomy or a diverting stoma when decompression fails or perforation occurs
Recurrent disease managed with routine rectal washouts, internal-sphincter botulinum toxin, and evaluation for an obstructive anatomical cause or residual aganglionosis
Paediatric surgical referral and intensive-care support for severe or septic episodes
